title: On inductive biases for the robust and interpretable prediction of drug concentrations using deep compartment models

content.abstract_summary: Extends the deep compartment model (DCM) architecture — a hybrid mechanistic-ML PK model — by introducing physiological inductive biases (boundary constraints, global parameter estimation, multi-branch networks) to improve robustness in sparse data settings. Validates on simulated haemophilia A data (756 patients from NHANES covariates) and real clinical data (69 patients, standard half-life FVIII). The multi-branch network architecture enables model interpretability through visualization of learned covariate functions, eliminating the need for post-hoc SHAP. Key finding: naive neural-ODE achieves the WORST performance on sparse real data; physiological constraints are necessary. Amsterdam UMC, published in JPKPD 2024.
key_findings: Naive DCM without constraints: 18% of models diverge on small data (N=20) producing physiologically implausible curves (peak FVIII up to 1340 IU/dL); global parameter constraints reduce divergence to 0.33% — constraints are not optional in sparse clinical settings

Neural-ODE (Lu et al. architecture) achieves the HIGHEST RMSE (worst performance) on real 69-patient sparse data (RMSE 19.5 IU/dL) vs multi-branch DCM 13.0 IU/dL and best NLME 13.7 IU/dL — contradict the narrative that neural-ODEs always outperform traditional methods; they fail with sparse data

Multi-branch network (separate sub-models per covariate) achieves lowest RMSE overall (13.0 IU/dL), outperforming the best previously published NLME model (13.7 IU/dL) — the only architecture that outperforms traditional pharmacometrics on this dataset

False covariates degrade performance: fully-connected DCM RMSE increases from 13.3 to 18.1 IU/dL when unimportant covariates added; multi-branch network less affected (15.6 IU/dL) — covariate selection is essential before fitting any DCM

Multi-branch architecture makes post-hoc explainability methods (SHAP) unnecessary: covariate effects are isolated by design and can be visualized directly — a cleaner approach to interpretability for regulatory purposes

Simulation study: 756 male NHANES individuals; 20-fold Monte Carlo CV × 5 model replicates = 100 replicates per condition; boundary constraints reduce divergence more than initialization but less than global parameter estimation
limitations: Haemophilia A with only 3 measurements per patient (4h, 24h, 48h) — extremely sparse; results may not generalize to drugs with richer PK sampling
Neural-ODE failure may be specific to the very sparse data setting (N=69, 3 obs/patient) — does not mean neural-ODE underperforms in general

Multi-branch architecture requires a priori specification of which covariates connect to which PK parameters — shifts complexity from model fitting to study design; in practice still requires pharmacometric expertise
Identifiability of neural components not formally analyzed; practical robustness is addressed via constraints but theoretical identifiability is not

extracted_claims.text: We conclude that physiological-based constraints can improve model robustness. We describe an interpretable architecture which aids model trust, which will be key for the adoption of machine learning-based models in clinical practice.

We show that all models were sensitive to learning false effects when trained in the presence of unimportant covariates, indicating the importance of selecting an appropriate set of covariates to link to the PK parameters.
Fully ML-based architectures, such as the Neural-ODE, greatly simplify model development but suffer when data is sparse.

numerical_findings.description: Real-world clinical validation dataset size (haemophilia A, 3 obs/patient)
RMSE on real data: multi-branch DCM vs best NLME vs naive DCM vs neural-ODE
Naive DCM divergence rate on small data (N=20)

gaps_addressed: Critical counter-evidence for M1.4 (when do hybrids NOT help?): neural-ODE underperforms traditional pharmacometrics on sparse real data — this nuanced finding is essential for a balanced WG scoping paper

Provides the architectural solution to practical identifiability in M1.3: physiological constraints reduce the solution space to realistic regions, directly analogous to prior distributions in Bayesian estimation

Multi-branch interpretability without SHAP is a concrete regulatory-readiness contribution — shows that hybrid models can be designed to be intrinsically interpretable rather than relying on post-hoc approximations
